candidates.title: Youth employment erosion in AI-exposed occupations
candidates.shift: Employment of young workers (22-25) in roles most exposed to AI automation is falling further below historical trend — now 19% below, up from 15% a year prior — even as overall labor markets remain stable.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative: if entry-level cognitive jobs keep thinning, this reshapes office occupancy patterns, corporate training footprints, and junior-staff housing/commuting demand — a demographic labor shift with delayed built-environment consequences.
candidates.evidence: Stanford Digital Economy Lab 'Canaries in the Coal Mine' study cited by Exponential View, showing AI-exposed youth employment trending further below baseline year-over-year.
candidates.initial_analysis: This is an early indicator of a shift from AI as a productivity tool to AI as a direct substitute for entry-level cognitive labor. Driven by rapid model capability gains in white-collar tasks, if sustained it would hollow out junior office roles, altering corporate real estate needs (less need for training floors, junior desks), entry-level housing/commuting demand near business districts, and the staffing/insurance models built around career-ladder employment.
candidates.author: Azeem Azhar
